findings.text: A dedicated allocation entry creates a guarded control stack region. It first requires platform support, then enforces flag, alignment and length rules before reserving space, and on request places an ordered capability token near the top so the region can later be adopted.

Creation rejects unknown option bits, rejects a start that is not page aligned, rejects a length of one word or any length not word aligned, page rounds the length and treats wrap as overflow, and propagates allocation failure directly without further action.

When token creation is requested the implementation reserves one trailing slot, or two when a marker is also requested, computes a capability value from the chosen slot address, stores it with a guarded control stack aware store, unmaps the whole region on store failure, and issues a control stack ordering barrier on success.

Status control distinguishes enable, query and lock. All three require platform support and reject compatibility threads. Enable rejects unknown bits, consults a lock check, forbids re enabling once a base or pointer was ever established, allows initial enable only for the current thread with fresh allocation and register update, and records mode with immediate effect for current. Query returns the stored mode. Lock accumulates bits including unknown future bits.

Guarded control stack paths fail safely on unsupported hardware, malformed arguments, overflowed rounding, allocation errors and token store faults with unmap. Re enable after prior use and cross thread enable are refused to avoid inconsistent register and memory state.

User fault resolution proceeds through locked lookup, permission and protection key checks, generic resolution, then outcome classification. Signals pending cause early exit with a kernel context detour. Completed work returns immediately because protection was already released. Retry marks the attempt as tried and repeats lookup. Other errors fall through to signal selection, with out of memory handled by invoking the killer and returning.

The fault path holds the address space read lock across region lookup and generic resolution. Permission mismatch and protection key mismatch release the lock before reporting access errors. Retry re enters lookup under the same discipline. The terminal error path releases before deciding the user signal, while the completed path returns without releasing because release already happened inside resolution.

Translation faults from the lower address range are treated as pageable faults while others go to the generic bad area path. Alignment faults prefer a compatibility fixup when that option is enabled and the context is compatibility, otherwise they also go to bad area. The generic bad handler reports failure. External abort and tag check paths normalize the fault address before reporting.

Fault reporting must cope with stale protection keys after concurrent permission changes, with faulty address tags being architecturally unknown for external aborts and tag checks, with validity indication suppressing the reported address, with firmware first handling that may defer work, and with machine check tainting plus precise signal selection among bus, machine check and segmentation variants.

Synchronous fault decoding uses a fixed dense table indexed by exception class. Each entry combines a handler routine with a signal number, an associated code, and a short diagnostic label describing level and category.

Entries pair a handler with a signal and code. Translation levels use do_translation_fault with SIGSEGV plus SEGV_MAPERR. Access flag and permission levels use do_page_fault with SIGSEGV plus SEGV_ACCERR. Synchronous external abort and walk and parity cases use do_sea with SIGBUS plus BUS_OBJERR or SIGKILL plus SI_KERNEL. Tag checks use do_tag_check_fault with SIGSEGV plus SEGV_MTESERR. Alignment uses do_alignment_fault with SIGBUS plus BUS_ADRALN. Address size and domain and unknown and most implementation cases use do_bad with SIGKILL plus SI_KERNEL, except one exclusive case with SIGBUS plus BUS_OBJERR.

A movable zeroed folio allocator is provided for fault time use. It starts from GFP_HIGHUSER_MOVABLE combined with __GFP_ZERO and adds __GFP_ZEROTAGS when the requesting region carries VM_MTE, then delegates to vma_alloc_folio for order zero at the faulting address.

Tag clearing for high pages first checks system_supports_mte and defers when tagging is unsupported. Otherwise for each page it checks try_page_mte_tagging with a once warning, uses mte_zero_clear_page_tags when clearing is requested and mte_clear_page_tags otherwise, marks via set_page_mte_tagged, and reports that the caller must not perform its own clearing.

Early fixed mapping storage uses boot page tables sized by the span from FIXADDR_TOT_START to FIXADDR_TOP at PMD_SHIFT and PUD_SHIFT granularities. Indexing subtracts the shifted base from the shifted address. Backing consists of bm_pte as a two dimensional leaf array plus bm_pmd and bm_pud kept in dedicated page table memory, with fixmap_pte selecting a leaf entry by table index and leaf index.

Fixed mapping installation checks the slot against FIX_HOLE and __end_of_fixed_addresses, resolves the virtual address via __fix_to_virt and its leaf entry via fixmap_pte, installs a physical mapping when protection is non empty and otherwise clears the entry and flushes one page via flush_tlb_kernel_range.
Fixed mapping installation traps on an out of range slot. Clearing a mapping always flushes the affected kernel range to avoid stale translations.
Tracing writes to user pages copy the supplied bytes and then, only when the region carries VM_EXEC, synchronize via sync_icache_aliases over exactly the destination range.
Persistent memory support offers writeback that orders via dmb osh and then cleans via dcache_clean_pop over the interval, plus invalidation via dcache_inval_poc over the interval.

Huge page support treats CONT_PMD_SIZE plus PMD_SIZE plus CONT_PTE_SIZE as always valid, and PUD_SIZE as valid only when pud_sect_supported holds and the middle level is not folded. The allocator order prefers PUD_SHIFT minus PAGE_SHIFT when sections are supported and otherwise CONT_PMD_SHIFT minus PAGE_SHIFT. Migration is supported exactly for valid sizes, warning on unrecognized sizes.

Contiguity helpers derive count and base granularity from size or from table alignment, distinguishing CONT_PMDS at PMD_SIZE versus CONT_PTES at PAGE_SIZE. Reading a huge entry returns the first constituent directly unless pte_present and pte_cont both hold, in which case pte_dirty and pte_young indications are folded across all siblings.

Atomic clear gathers dirty and young indications across the whole contiguous span while clearing. Flushing variants additionally purge via __flush_hugetlb_tlb_range with TLBF_NOWALKCACHE, with a kernel split using flush_tlb_kernel_range for the non huge helper. Installation writes non present spans directly and otherwise uses break before make when replacing a valid contiguous entry.

Huge table management walks from the top level allocating missing intermediates, then selects the entry level by requested size with sharing for discrete middle pages and alignment checks for contiguous sizes. Lookup checks presence at each level, treats leaf or swapped upper entries as terminal, applies CONT_PMD_MASK and CONT_PTE_MASK for contiguous probes, and returns the appropriate level or null. Tail masking, entry construction with huge and contiguous markers, and per constituent clearing follow the same size classification with warnings on mismatch.

An additional helper to atomically read and clear a huge entry is declared with at least address space and address parameters; the remainder of its signature and its behavior are not visible in the routed span.
